# Springs and gestures (house standards, version 4)

<!-- generated by tools/build_data.py from synthesis/; edit the source, not this file -->

Springs for motion a finger drives, interruptible animation, velocity handoff, momentum projection, rubber-banding, drag mechanics and feedback on the causal frame.

Rules from non-negotiable sources. **must**: never break it without the person's explicit override. **should**: the default; say so when you depart from it. How to change one: `../standards.md`.

### STD-springs-gestures-01: Springs for anything a finger drives
**must**. Animate drags, flicks, swipes and any other gesture the user can interrupt or reverse mid-motion with a spring, not with a fixed-duration transition or @keyframes; motion no finger started or can interrupt runs on timing (an easing curve plus a duration).
- Why: Springs start from the current value and carry velocity through an interruption, while timing curves restart; a pre-scripted, fixed-duration animation cannot respond to new input. Non-gesture UI that is triggered rapidly only needs a CSS transition (STD-springs-gestures-15).
- Sources: S-L19-016, S-L19-020, S-L19-020, S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-033, S-L19-025, S-L19-017, S-L19-024, S-L19-032

### STD-springs-gestures-02: Define springs by damping and response
**should**. Specify each spring with two designer parameters, damping ratio (or bounce) and response (or duration), rather than mass, stiffness and damping, and never treat response as a fixed duration.
- Values: damping-ratio: 1.0 = critically damped, no bounce, smooth settle. < 1.0 = overshoots and oscillates.; response: how quickly the value reaches the target, in seconds; motion-apple-style: { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }; motion-traditional-physics (only for more control): { type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }
- Why: Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet with these two designer-friendly parameters, and Emil recommends the duration-and-bounce form as easier to reason about. A spring has no fixed duration: its settle time emerges from the parameters.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-023, S-L19-033, S-L19-025, S-L19-018

### STD-springs-gestures-04: Default springs are critically damped
**must**. Default every UI spring to critically damped (damping ratio 1.0, no overshoot) with a response of 0.3–0.4 s, and move or reposition elements with damping 1.0 and response 0.4 s; only a spring that follows a momentum gesture (STD-springs-gestures-06) or a deliberately playful or decorative moment (STD-springs-gestures-07, STD-springs-gestures-45) may be under-damped.
- Values: damping-ratio: 1.0; response: 0.3–0.4; move-reposition: Move / reposition (e.g. PiP) | 1.0 | 0.4; motion: { type: 'spring', bounce: 0, duration: 0.4 }; reanimated: { duration: 400, dampingRatio: 1 }
- Why: Critically damped motion is graceful and non-distracting; the source calls damping 1.0 springs everywhere by default a safe house style, and 1.0 / 0.4 is what Apple ships for move / reposition.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-020, S-L19-020, S-L19-016

### STD-springs-gestures-05: Bounce only after a momentum gesture
**must**. Never let a spring overshoot on UI that appears or moves without a gesture behind it (a menu fading in, a popover, a dialog, a plain reposition); keep bounce for motion that follows a gesture that carried momentum (a flick, a throw, a drag release) and, beyond that, only for deliberately playful interactions and rare delight moments.
- Why: Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong; overshoot on a card you flicked feels right. Emil's skills also reserve bounce for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions and keep it out of most UI.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-020, S-L19-016, S-L19-018, S-L19-024

### STD-springs-gestures-06: Momentum spring for released drags
**should**. Settle or snap back a released drag with a slightly under-damped spring (damping ratio about 0.8, bounce 0.2) started from the release velocity; a settle that must stop at a hard edge, such as a sheet dismissing off-screen, stays critically damped and clamped instead (STD-springs-gestures-10).
- Values: apple: damping ~0.8, response 0.3–0.4; motion-apple-design: { type: 'spring', bounce: 0.2, duration: 0.4 }; motion-animate-recipe: { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }; reanimated: { duration: 400, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity }
- Why: Settling with a spring lets an interrupted drag keep its velocity, and a little bounce is right only because a flick preceded it. The sources give 0.4 s (Apple, Reanimated) and 0.5 s (Emil's web recipe) for this spring, and the Expo recipes spring a dismissed sheet and a swipe-to-delete row that returns home at dampingRatio 1, so 0.8 is the default, not a rule.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-020, S-L19-017, S-L19-016, S-L19-024

### STD-springs-gestures-07: Keep bounce subtle, 0.1 to 0.3
**must**. When a spring bounces, keep bounce between 0.1 and 0.3, and keep bounce out of most UI, reserving it for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions.
- Values: bounce: 0.1–0.3
- Why: The sources ask for subtle bounce and say to avoid it in most UI contexts.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Spring bounce above 0.3: keep it at 0.1–0.3, and only after a momentum gesture.
- Sources: S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-033, S-L19-025, S-L19-024

### STD-springs-gestures-08: Sheet and drawer spring values
**must**. Drive a sheet or drawer's spring with damping ratio 0.8 and response 0.3 s (Reanimated: { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity }), about 300ms perceived, and hand it the release velocity; the dismissal spring is the exception and stays critically damped and clamped at the screen edge (STD-springs-gestures-10). The web drag-to-dismiss recipe settles with { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }.
- Values: apple: Drawer / sheet | 0.8 | 0.3; reanimated: { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity }; perceived-duration: ~300ms; dismissal: { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 1, velocity: e.velocityY, overshootClamping: true }; web-recipe: { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }
- Why: These are the values Apple ships for drawer / sheet, and the animate-expo spring and duration tables give sheets and drawers a spring of about 300ms perceived; the Expo sheet recipe dismisses with dampingRatio 1 and overshootClamping. On the web, Emil's drawer (Vaul) opens and closes with a 500ms cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) CSS transition instead, so this spring is not the web drawer's open and close motion.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-016, S-L19-016, S-L19-015, S-L19-015, S-L19-017

### STD-springs-gestures-09: Spring values for rotating elements
**should**. Rotate elements with a spring of damping ratio 0.8 and response 0.4 s.
- Values: damping: 0.8; response: 0.4
- Why: These are the values Apple ships for rotation.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-10: Clamp springs at hard edges
**must** · react-native. Add overshootClamping: true to any spring that must not pass a hard edge, including a sheet's dismissal spring.
- Values: clamp: overshootClamping: true; sheet-dismissal: withSpring(HEIGHT, { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 1, velocity: e.velocityY, overshootClamping: true })
- Why: Otherwise the sheet springs past the bottom of the screen and flashes a gap.
- Sources: S-L19-016, S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-11: Independent X and Y springs
**should**. Animate two-dimensional motion with two independent springs, one for X and one for Y, not one spring on the 2D distance.
- Why: A single spring on a 2D distance desyncs when X and Y have different velocities.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-12: Every animation can be grabbed mid-flight
**must**. Make every animation the user triggers or touches interruptible and redirectable at any moment: a user can grab a moving element mid-flight and reverse it, and a closing modal or sheet that is grabbed again follows the finger instead of finishing its close first.
- Why: Interruptibility is the single most important principle, because the thought and the gesture happen in parallel; for anything a finger touches it is the baseline, not polish.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-016, S-L19-011, S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-13: Never block input during transitions
**must**. Never lock out input while a transition runs, a stagger included: the items must be usable before the cascade finishes.
- Why: Every animation must be interruptible and redirectable at any moment.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-017, S-L19-023, S-L19-033, S-L19-025, S-L19-024

### STD-springs-gestures-14: Start from the on-screen value
**must**. When an animation is interrupted or a drag begins, start from the element's live on-screen (presentation) value, never from its target or logical value.
- Values: reanimated-onStart: context.set(translateY.get())
- Why: Starting from the logical or target value causes a visible jump; without it, grabbing a sheet mid-animation teleports it.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-015, S-L19-016

### STD-springs-gestures-15: Transitions, not keyframes, for rapid UI
**must** · css, web, react. Animate anything that can be triggered rapidly or reversed mid-motion (stacking toasts, toggles, expand/collapse, list add and remove) with CSS transitions or springs, never @keyframes.
- Values: example: transition: transform 400ms ease
- Why: Transitions retarget from the current value while keyframes restart from zero; with keyframes, older toasts jump into their new position instead of moving smoothly.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Keyframes restart from zero: animate toasts and toggles with a CSS transition or a spring.
- Sources: S-L19-006, S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033, S-L19-024

### STD-springs-gestures-16: Carry velocity through a reversal
**must**. When a gesture reverses direction mid-animation, carry the current velocity through the re-target instead of cutting to a new animation (on the web, use a spring library that re-targets from the current velocity).
- Why: Replacing one animation with another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity, a 'brick wall'; iOS avoids it natively with additive animations.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-17: Hand the release velocity to the spring
**must**. When a gesture ends, pass the pointer's release velocity to the spring as its initial velocity, so the motion continues at the finger's exact speed.
- Values: motion: absolute px/s velocity directly (velocity option); relative-velocity: relativeVelocity = gestureVelocity / (targetValue − currentValue); relative-example: element at y=50, target y=150 (100px to go), finger moving 50px/s → initial spring velocity = 50 / 100 = 0.5; reanimated: velocity: e.velocityY
- Why: Then there is no visible seam between dragging and animating; the sources call it the detail that most separates 'fluid' from 'fine'.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-020, S-L19-015, S-L19-016

### STD-springs-gestures-18: Record pointer history for velocity
**should** · web. While dragging, record the positions and timestamps of the last few pointermove events, not just the current point, so the velocity is known at release.
- Why: You will need the velocity at release.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-19: Project the flick, then snap
**must**. On release, project where the flick would come to rest with Apple's exponential-decay function (the current position plus project(velocity)) and decide the outcome from that projected point, never from the release point or a distance-only threshold: snap to the snap point nearest the projection, so a hard flick can skip points or close a drawer, and commit a dismiss or delete when the projection passes its threshold.
- Values: project: (initialVelocity / 1000) * decelerationRate / (1 - decelerationRate); projected-endpoint: currentPosition + project(releaseVelocity); decelerationRate: ≈ 0.998 for normal scroll feel; 0.99 for snappier; do-not-use: v²/(2·decel)
- Why: This is what makes a flick feel like it throws the element, like scroll deceleration: a fast short swipe commits and a slow long one does not. The physics-textbook v²/(2·decel) is not what Apple ships.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-015, S-L19-005, S-L19-016

### STD-springs-gestures-20: Velocity sign decides commit or reverse
**should**. At release, decide whether a gesture commits or reverses by the sign of its velocity, not by its position.
- Why: The source's quick reference gives velocity sign, not position, as the way to decide reverse versus commit.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-21: A flick is enough to dismiss
**must**. Dismiss a swiped or dragged element when its distance passes the threshold OR its velocity (absolute distance divided by the milliseconds since the drag started) exceeds about 0.11; never require distance alone.
- Values: velocity: Math.abs(swipeAmount) / timeTaken; condition: Math.abs(swipeAmount) >= SWIPE_THRESHOLD || velocity > 0.11; velocity-threshold: 0.11
- Why: A quick, short swipe should dismiss: people should not have to drag past a fixed point. Sonner's 0.11 was found by trial and error, against the average speed since the drag started, not the instantaneous release velocity [inferred].
- Sources: S-L19-006, S-L19-005, S-L19-023, S-L19-017, S-L19-033, S-L19-025, S-L19-024, S-L19-016, S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-22: Sheets dismiss on projected position
**must** · react-native. Decide a draggable sheet's dismissal by its projected position (current position plus project(velocityY)), not by the distance travelled: dismiss when the projection passes 40% of the sheet's height.
- Values: projected: translateY.get() + project(e.velocityY); threshold: HEIGHT * 0.4
- Why: Velocity decides, not distance: a quick flick dismisses even a few pixels down, while requiring 40% travel makes the sheet feel heavy.
- Sources: S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-23: Swipe-to-delete commits on projection
**should** · react-native. For a row that reveals action buttons, use gesture-handler's ReanimatedSwipeable; build the gesture yourself only for swipe-to-commit. Commit a swipe-to-delete row when its projected position passes the threshold, sliding it out with withTiming(-WIDTH, { duration: 200, easing: EASE_OUT }) and deleting only when that finishes; otherwise spring it home with { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 1, velocity: e.velocityX }.
- Values: commit: withTiming(-WIDTH, { duration: 200, easing: EASE_OUT }, (f) => { if (f) scheduleOnRN(onDelete, id); }); EASE_OUT: Easing.bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1); spring-back: withSpring(0, { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 1, velocity: e.velocityX }); swipe-to-reveal: ReanimatedSwipeable (react-native-gesture-handler)
- Why: ReanimatedSwipeable already handles thresholds, overshoot and open/close on the UI thread. A committed swipe slides off with a short ease-out and the delete runs only when it finishes; an uncommitted one springs home with the release velocity.
- Sources: S-L19-015, S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-24: Sequential snap points when all matter
**should** · react. When every snap point of a drawer is equally important, disable velocity-based snapping (Vaul: snapToSequentialPoint) so a fast drag cannot skip a point.
- Values: vaul-prop: snapToSequentialPoint
- Why: The Vaul docs offer it for drawers whose snap points are all equally important. This is a good-to-have source, and learn/sources.json records that Vaul's README says the library is unmaintained, so treat this as a pattern, not a dependency recommendation.
- Sources: S-L19-098

### STD-springs-gestures-25: Rubber-band at edges, never hard-stop
**must**. When a drag goes past a boundary, or in a direction that does not dismiss, let the element follow with progressively rising resistance (rubberband with constant 0.55) instead of stopping it dead.
- Values: rubberband: (overshoot * dimension * constant) / (dimension + constant * Math.abs(overshoot)); constant: 0.55
- Why: A hard stop reads as frozen, while continuous resistance reads as responsive but with nothing more there; real things slow down before they stop.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-015, S-L19-016, S-L19-017, S-L19-023, S-L19-033, S-L19-025, S-L19-024, S-L19-005, S-L19-006

### STD-springs-gestures-26: Track the pointer 1:1 throughout
**must**. For a drag, slider, drawer or sheet, update the UI 1:1 with the pointer for the whole interaction, keeping the element glued to the finger at the offset where it was grabbed (never snap its center to the pointer); never animate only when the gesture completes.
- Values: grab-offset: grabOffset = e.clientY - el.getBoundingClientRect().top
- Why: Feedback must be continuous during the interaction, not just at the end.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-28: Capture the pointer during a drag
**must** · web. Once a drag starts, capture the pointer (setPointerCapture on pointerdown) so the drag continues when the pointer leaves the element.
- Values: api: el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId)
- Why: Otherwise the drag stops as soon as the mouse or thumb moves outside the element.
- Sources: S-L19-006, S-L19-017, S-L19-023, S-L19-033, S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-30: Commit to a drag axis after 10px
**must**. Require about 10px of movement along the gesture's axis before a drag or swipe takes over, then track 1:1, and always declare that axis on a pan inside a scroll view.
- Values: threshold: ~10px; vertical-pan: activeOffsetY([-10, 10]); horizontal-pan: activeOffsetX([-10, 10])
- Why: The threshold requires intent before committing and lets a swipe on the other axis win; a pan with no axis inside a scroll view steals vertical scrolls and the list feels broken.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-015, S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-34: Derive linked visuals from the drag
**should**. Drive everything that follows a drag (backdrop opacity, the background's scale and corner radius) from the same drag value or drag progress, not from separate animations.
- Values: example: Dragging the drawer down by 40% will change the border radius to 60% of its max value; reanimated: interpolate(translateY.get(), [0, HEIGHT], [1, 0], Extrapolation.CLAMP)
- Why: Values tied to drag progress stay in sync and cost nothing extra.
- Sources: S-L19-005, S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-39: Recognize gestures continuously, in parallel
**should**. Track every plausible gesture in parallel from the first move and cancel the losers once intent is clear; do not use recognizers that only report a final state (swipeleft-type events).
- Why: Final-state recognizers throw away the continuous tracking you need for feedback.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Final-state swipe recognizer: track the pointer continuously (a pan) and decide on release.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-41: Remove latency from the input path
**must**. Audit every latency on the input path (debounces, artificial timers, transition waits, the ~300ms tap delay) and remove anything that is not essential.
- Values: tap-delay: ~300ms
- Why: The moment lag appears, the feeling of directness falls off a cliff; anything non-essential on the input path is a regression.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-42: Hint in the gesture's direction
**should**. Make intermediate frames point toward the outcome (for example growing up and out toward the finger) rather than interpolating blindly to the end state.
- Why: Humans predict a final state from a trajectory.
- Sources: S-L19-020

### STD-springs-gestures-45: Spring-smooth decorative mouse tracking
**should** · react, web. Pass decorative mouse-tracking values through a spring (Motion's useSpring) instead of tying the visual directly to the pointer position.
- Values: example: useSpring(mouseX * 0.1, { stiffness: 100, damping: 10 })
- Why: Tying visual changes directly to mouse position feels artificial because it lacks motion; a spring adds momentum.
- Sources: S-L19-023, S-L19-033

### STD-springs-gestures-59: Feedback fires on the causal event
**must**. Fire motion, sound and haptic feedback on the actual causal event (the toggle flipping, the item snapping home, the detent catching), not when an animation finishes, and match its character to the physicality of the action.
- Values: react-native-tab-example: Haptics.selectionAsync() on the press, not when the pill lands; from-worklet: scheduleOnRN(Haptics.selectionAsync)
- Why: It must be obvious what caused the feedback.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-016, S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-60: Visual, sound and haptic share a frame
**must**. Fire the visual, the sound and the haptic in the same frame; never let a CSS transition lag the audio or haptic.
- Why: Latency between them destroys the illusion, and a haptic that lags its animation reads as a glitch, not as feedback.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-016, S-L19-015

### STD-springs-gestures-61: Haptics and sound only when meaningful
**must**. Reserve haptics and sound for meaningful moments (success, error, commit, snap), and fire at most one haptic per user action: never on scroll, never per frame, never on an entrance animation the user did not cause.
- Values: moments: success, error, commit, snap
- Why: Over-feedback trains users to ignore all of it; used everywhere, users turn haptics off.
- Sources: S-L19-020, S-L19-016

### STD-springs-gestures-63: Blur or stretch very fast motion
**should**. For very fast motion, add a subtle motion blur or stretch along the direction of travel rather than moving a hard, sharp edge.
- Why: A subtle blur or stretch encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak; smoothness is about what is in the frames, not just the frame rate.
- Sources: S-L19-020
